newsitem.title: ITALY: Festive Italy markets sobered by German EMU doubts.
newsitem.headline: Festive Italy markets sobered by German EMU doubts.

text.p: German sobriety over prospects for forming a single European currency is draining some of the spirit from Italy's mercurial bond market and could keep convergence optimism muted for a while, economists said.

Comments from a German government adviser and research body Ifo on a possible delay to economic and monetary union (EMU) and Italy's suitability to join at the 1999 start have kept the brakes on Btps after a period of relentless gains.

Dollar strength is also prodding investors to ponder whether Germany might raise interest rates, the effect of such a move on Italy and whether the U.S. currency might throw Italy's hard-won suppression of inflation off course.

"We're going to get more of this in the next few weeks. It will be a bumpy road -- maybe the market can recover at times but the trend that we see at the moment is for a wider spread above these levels," said Lorenzo Stanca at Credito Italiano.
The yield spread of the benchmark 10-year Btp over the benchmark Bund splayed out to 98 basis points in early trade on Tuesday and was sitting at 96 by midsession.

The spread has come in dramatically over the last few months and narrowed to a record level of 80 last week as investors continued to buy Italian debt on the expectation that EMU will start on time with Italy in at the debut.
Stanca said he expected the spread to remain between 90 and 110 short term and then saw it out at 100-120 in September when the government's 1998 budget preparations enter the final straight.
The September Btp future on LIFFE was at 137.43 by 1310 GMT, six basis points down on the day after rallying to record levels since early June, with only one real pause in mid-July.

Bonn government adviser Rolf Peffekoven, one of the country's 'wise men', recommended a two year delay to EMU while the Ifo institute said while Italy might meet a key deficit requirement for joining the single currency, it should still be kept out of the EMU start on grounds of sustainability.
Stephen King, chief European economist at HSBC in London, said he did not think the German concerns would build into anything dramatic yet.
"There is more risk of things going wrong in the first quarter of next year but I would see this as no more than a temporary interruption at this point," King said.
Germans' aversion to Italy as a primary EMU bedmate is well documented but Stanca said objections would be made louder and clearer as debate on who joins and who doesn't gets underway.
Germany is also the root of another concern. With the dollar soaring against European currencies including the mark and lira, analysts see the chance that German interest rates might rise.

Riccardo Barbieri at Morgan Stanley in London said sentiment was shifting on the risk of a hike but he added: "I don't see that as a problem for Italy. There is still a differential of 400 basis points in overnight rates between Italy and Germany."
"It would be unrealistic to expect that by the start of EMU, if Italy participates, then all those 400 basis points would come from lower Italian rates," he said.
King said while monetary tightening was a risk, Germany's domestic economic situation did not justify a significant rise.
The dollar's climb to a 12-year high against the lira has also provoked talk about the impact on Italian consumer prices, which are growing at about 1.6 percent year-on-year this month.
Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi played down the U.S. currency's effect, saying it would not lead to an inflation spiral. Economists were also sanguine about import prices.
"If the dollar stays where it is now then inflation in 1998 would be 0.3-0.4 higher than it would otherwise be. That's not tremendous - and it'll be the same for Germany," Stanca said.
